RESULTS_PARA_RANDOM: *Random folds.* On Task A the four models are statistically tied: their mean macro-F1 ranges from 0.909 to 0.917, and none of the nine project-bootstrap intervals for a transformer minus the SVM excludes zero. On Task B the transformers pull ahead. RoBERTa reaches 0.913 ± 0.024 and DistilBERT 0.892 ± 0.016, against 0.821 ± 0.015 for the SVM; their intervals exclude zero in three and two of three seeds respectively. BERT (0.858 ± 0.004) is ahead of the SVM on average, but none of its intervals excludes zero.
RESULTS_PARA_PROJECT: *Project-held-out folds.* Holding out whole projects lowers every score (right-hand columns of [[tab:res]] and [[fig:res]]), but not equally. On Task A the SVM loses 32 points of macro-F1 and ends at 0.590 ± 0.013, whereas the transformers lose 11–17 points: DistilBERT reaches 0.736 ± 0.024, BERT 0.765 ± 0.010 and RoBERTa 0.806 ± 0.028. Eight of the nine project-bootstrap intervals exclude zero; the exception is DistilBERT with seed 42 (difference 0.108, 95% interval −0.029 to 0.229). Most of the loss is in the functional class. Averaged over seeds, functional recall falls to 0.27 for the SVM, 0.53 for DistilBERT, 0.56 for BERT and 0.67 for RoBERTa, while non-functional recall stays at 0.93 or above for every model. On an unseen project the models therefore label many functional requirements as non-functional; even the best model finds only about two thirds of them. A likely but untested reason is that functional requirements are written in each project's domain vocabulary, whereas quality requirements reuse phrases such as “shall be available” or “within 2 seconds” across projects. Task B loses less: the SVM drops to 0.718 ± 0.001, DistilBERT reaches 0.825 ± 0.022 and RoBERTa 0.810 ± 0.018, and both are ahead of the SVM in every seed. BERT (0.774 ± 0.002) is again ahead on average without any interval excluding zero. The drop should not be read as the effect of unseen projects alone, because the protocols differ in other ways. Five project-held-out folds train on about 80% of the items, against 90% for ten random folds (on Task A, 409–600 training items per fold instead of about 562). The folds are also uneven, because PROMISE projects differ in size and content: Task A test folds hold between 25 and 216 items, and projects 11–15 contain no functional requirements at all.
RESULTS_PARA_CAL: *Calibration and the confidence gate.* The raw softmax scores were over-confident on unseen projects. On Task A project-held-out folds the expected calibration error (ECE) of the three transformers was 0.16–0.19, and a threshold of 0.95 on the raw scores would have auto-labelled 82%–91% of the items at a precision of only 0.81–0.85. BERT was badly calibrated on Task B as well (ECE 0.27–0.30, against 0.11 or less for DistilBERT and RoBERTa). Cross-fitted temperature scaling reduced the Task A project-held-out ECE to 0.04–0.05, but it also showed how little of that task can be automated safely: after scaling, no Task A item of an unseen project reached a confidence of 0.95, and the cross-fitted threshold auto-labelled at most 22% of the items (RoBERTa), at a precision of 0.82, short of the 0.95 target. Task B behaved better. With the cross-fitted threshold, DistilBERT auto-labelled 53% of the unseen-project items at a precision of 0.95, RoBERTa 65% at 0.93 and BERT 30% at 0.91; the remaining items would go to review. Under random folds the same procedure auto-labelled about 88% of Task A items at a precision of 0.95, which again shows how optimistic random splits are.
RESULTS_PARA_EXT: *External test.* Trained on all of PROMISE with its original labels and applied to the 327 industrial requirements, the SVM reached a macro-F1 of 0.638 on the 246 items that have only a functional or only a quality aspect. The transformers reached 0.708 ± 0.076 (DistilBERT), 0.711 ± 0.072 (BERT) and 0.719 ± 0.094 (RoBERTa), and the within-document bootstrap put their seed-averaged advantage over the SVM at +0.070 to +0.081, with every interval excluding zero. The large standard deviations come mostly from seed 44, which gave 0.612–0.628 for all three transformers against 0.722–0.790 for seeds 42 and 43. Training on the relabelled PROMISE instead changed little for the SVM, DistilBERT and BERT (all intervals for the difference include zero), but it raised RoBERTa to 0.781 ± 0.033, a gain of 0.062 (95% interval 0.030 to 0.093). As a quality flag over all 327 items, every model reached an F1 between 0.67 and 0.71. The errors differ, however: with the original labels the transformers flagged 33%–34% of the purely functional items as having a quality aspect, against 45% for the SVM, and flagged 59%–60% of the mixed F+Q items. Results also varied by document. RoBERTa reached 0.78 on Leeds and 0.78 on ReqView, but only 0.45 on Dronology and 0.40 on WASP, where only 2 and 6 items are purely quality requirements, so those two values rest on very few items.
RESULTS_PARA_TRANSFER: The calibration did not transfer well. With the temperature fitted on the PROMISE out-of-fold predictions of the same model and seed, the external ECE fell from 0.16–0.35 to 0.07–0.23, so the scores stayed miscalibrated. A threshold for 0.95 precision could be set on PROMISE in eight of the nine runs. Applied unchanged to the external items, it auto-labelled 12%–44% of them (30–109 items) at a precision of 0.82–1.00, and met the target in only 5 of the 8 runs; the three failures were the seed-44 runs of all three transformers.
RESULTS_PARA_LLM: *Zero-shot LLM.* Without any training, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct reached a macro-F1 of 0.408 on Task A, because it called only 8% of the requirements non-functional although 59% are. On Task B it reached 0.716, about the same as the SVM on unseen projects. On the external items it flagged only 4% of the items with a quality aspect (macro-F1 0.530). A model of this size with one fixed prompt is a weak baseline, and larger models or few-shot prompts may do much better; we did not test them.
ABSTRACT_RESULT: On random folds all models tied on functional versus non-functional classification (macro-F1 0.909–0.917). On unseen projects every score fell, but the transformers fell less (0.736–0.806 versus 0.590 for the SVM; project-bootstrap intervals excluded zero in eight of nine runs). On the industrial requirements they led the SVM by 0.070–0.081 macro-F1, but confidence thresholds set on PROMISE met their precision target in only 5 of 8 runs.
DISC_RESULT: Under random folds a linear TF-IDF model was as good as any transformer for the coarse FR/NFR decision, whereas RoBERTa and DistilBERT were clearly better at separating quality classes. Moving to project-held-out folds cost the SVM 32 points of macro-F1 on Task A but the transformers only 11–17, part of which may come from smaller training sets and uneven test folds rather than from unseen projects alone. The transformers' advantage is therefore largest where it matters for adoption, on projects they have not seen, which agrees with the unseen-project results of NoRBERT {{hey2020norbert;hey2022corrected}}. The external test points the same way, with a smaller margin: on documents written by other teams and labelled by other researchers, the transformers stayed ahead of the SVM, but their scores (0.708–0.719) were far below the random-fold numbers and varied strongly with the seed and the document. Two cautions follow. BERT-base, the original model of the family, was the weakest transformer on Task B and the worst calibrated, so the choice of encoder matters even within one family. And calibration is not portable: temperature scaling fixed most of the miscalibration on held-out PROMISE folds, but a threshold chosen on PROMISE missed its precision target on the external documents in 3 of 8 runs. For a team, the practical consequence is that any model, and especially its confidence threshold, should be re-checked on the team's own items before its labels are trusted.
CONCL_RESULT: on random folds the fully fine-tuned DistilBERT, BERT and RoBERTa were no better than a linear SVM at separating functional from non-functional requirements (macro-F1 0.909–0.917), but RoBERTa and DistilBERT were clearly better at telling the four most frequent quality classes apart. When whole projects were held out, every model lost ground, and the first task changed from a statistical tie to a clear transformer lead (0.736–0.806 against 0.590). On 327 industrial requirements from four other projects the transformers kept a smaller lead over the SVM, and its bootstrap intervals excluded zero. Even so, the best model found only about two thirds of the functional requirements of an unseen project, and confidence thresholds did not carry over from PROMISE to new documents, so a confidence gate needs calibration on the team's own items before it can be trusted.
